posts.note: Long essay arguing psychedelic-assisted therapy lacks evidence that the therapy component matters. Mostly past analysis of MDMA, psilocybin, ibogaine and ketamine trials; four hedged forward-looking claims logged.

History and brain-circuit review of depersonalization plus TMS case for an RCT. One cynical public-health forecast, one counterfactual conditional, one normative RCT call, and the Radial boilerplate logged.
Review of cannabis and suicide risk data; present-tense risk claims only. Only the Radial boilerplate ('additional locations coming soon') is forward-looking.
Effect-size explainer (Skee-Lo height conversion). Only the Radial boilerplate is forward-looking.
Child sexual abuse prevalence essay. Two future-tense prevalence or bet statements logged for recall with low forecast value, plus one conditional closing claim.
AdCom 10-1 vote against Otsuka/Lundbeck brexpiprazole/sertraline for PTSD. One implicit regulatory call, one future-tense prevalence statistic, and the Radial boilerplate.
Parody legal filing (Lord of the Rings). Fictional damages claims only; nothing reads as a sincere real-world expectation.
Coldplay kiss-cam framing of bipolar mania symptoms. Descriptive and educational; the 'probably not what was going on' line is retrospective speculation, not a forecast.

statements.quote: Either way, well-designed studies will suss out the truth, if we will allow dispassionate science to do what it does best—tease out cause and effect, even when it’s difficult.
statements.context: Closing lines of an essay arguing there is no robust evidence that psychotherapy is a necessary component of psychedelic or ketamine treatment. The author expects that well-designed trials (drug with versus without therapy) will settle whether therapy adds anything, conditional on 'dispassionate science' being allowed to run such trials.
statements.note: Conditional ('if we will allow'); no date. Generic expectation that future trials will resolve the therapy question.

statements.quote: I don’t see any reason why post-treatment psychotherapy, when paired with the needs of the patient, should be any less effective than these treatments already are.
statements.context: Section on the plausibility of psychotherapy after (not during) psychedelic dosing. The author expects post-treatment psychotherapy paired with a psychedelic to be at least as effective as psychotherapy paired with existing antidepressants such as Prozac or Zoloft, which he says get better outcomes when therapy is added.
statements.confidence_phrase: I don’t see any reason why
statements.note: Hedged expectation about the efficacy of a not-yet-tested sequence (psychedelic, then therapy); no trial or date named.

statements.quote: Still, despite the remarkable promise this compound —perhaps above all others—holds to relieve profound human suffering, it’s really, really hard to argue that the therapy could assist much during the process.
statements.context: Ibogaine section ('Ibogaine: (head shake)'). Compound claim: ibogaine holds remarkable promise, perhaps above all other psychedelic compounds, to relieve profound human suffering; and therapy is unlikely to assist during the ibogaine experience itself, because patients need cardiac telemetry, an escort to the bathroom, and sit with an eye mask on.
statements.confidence_phrase: remarkable promise; really, really hard to argue that the therapy could assist
statements.note: Compound claim: promise of ibogaine plus doubt that in-session therapy helps. Both undated potential claims.

statements.quote: All of these studies established that psilocybin may be a useful treatment, and all of them chose to have somebody else around while the alteration of consciousness was occurring.
statements.context: Psilocybin section. After citing the COMP360 trials, an NYU alcohol use disorder study and Compass/veteran PTSD studies, the author summarizes that psilocybin may be a useful treatment, while noting that none of the trials separated the drug from 'psychological support'.
statements.note: Evidence summary with a hedged predictive reading ('may be a useful treatment'); low forecast value.

statements.quote: But this is not the world we live in—we will spend endless time ignoring the causes of problems, and pouring gas on fires.
statements.context: After noting that child sexual abuse and youth cannabis use are the main drivers of depersonalization, the author says a just world would focus on prevention, then predicts society will instead keep ignoring the causes ('Public health is so last year!'). Cynical forecast about public-health priorities, used to justify focusing on treatment (TMS).
statements.note: Rhetorical, cynical forecast about society; no date, no measurable target.

statements.quote: In a just world, we would be focusing on the prevention of the abuse of children, and that would do away with a substantial portion, along with reducing cannabis use in youth, of associated conditions that may be fuel for the fire.
statements.context: Same passage. Counterfactual conditional: if society prevented child abuse and reduced youth cannabis use, a substantial portion of associated conditions (depersonalization among them) would go away. The next sentence says this is not the world we live in.
statements.note: Counterfactual conditional; the author treats the antecedent as unrealistic. Low forecast value.

statements.quote: Is it about time to get the clinical trial show on the road? Yes. Yes, it is.
statements.context: End of the TMS section on depersonalization/derealization disorder (DPD). After reviewing single-session rTMS studies of the TPJ and VLPFC, a 2021 systematic review calling TPJ stimulation 'promising', and an open-label VLPFC case series (average 44% CDS reduction), and noting no one has run the RCT yet, the author calls for the randomized controlled trial to start now.
statements.note: Normative call for an RCT; predictive reading only implicit (author expects VLPFC/TPJ rTMS to help DPD). Logged for recall.

statements.quote: One in five girls will be a victim of child sexual abuse.
statements.context: Essay framing Jeffrey Epstein as a symptom of a public-health-scale child sexual abuse (CSA) problem. The author states the prevalence of CSA as one in five girls (and one in twenty boys), citing Finkelhor et al. 2009 and the National Center for Victims of Crime, and compares it with cardiovascular disease prevalence in New York State.
entities: National Center for Victims of Crime
statements.note: Prevalence statistic phrased in future tense; restates cited data, not a forecast of change. Low forecast value.

statements.quote: And I’m willing to bet it causes more suffering to endlessly hear, on the news, that hundreds to thousands of adult humans who paid-to-perpetrate are casually strolling around, scott-free.
statements.context: The author argues that endless news coverage of Epstein's clients going unpunished causes additional suffering to CSA survivors (over 20% of the audience, by his estimate). 'I'm willing to bet' carries the confidence; the claim concerns a present, ongoing effect rather than a future event.
statements.note: Confidence phrase 'I'm willing to bet' but about a present causal effect; logged for recall.

statements.quote: Because child sexual abuse is a plague on the house of humanity, and even a semblance of justice for the victims won’t undo that. It would, however, be a nice start.
statements.context: Closing of the Epstein essay, answering 'Why are we talking about Jeffrey Epstein?'. The author says CSA is a plague on humanity and that even a semblance of justice for the victims would not undo that harm, though it would be a start.
statements.note: Conditional negative claim (justice, if it comes, will not undo the harm); low forecast value.

statements.quote: This is one that (probably) didn’t clear the bar. The advisory committee vote isn’t binding, but the overwhelming majority were clear in their decision—the data isn’t there yet.
statements.context: The FDA advisory committee (CDER) voted 10-1 against Otsuka/Lundbeck's brexpiprazole/sertraline (Rexulti plus Zoloft) supplemental application for PTSD; only one of two Phase III trials separated from placebo and the FDA usually requires two replicated trials. The author judges the application probably did not clear the bar and notes the vote is not binding, implying he expects the FDA to decline the application.
statements.note: Implicit regulatory call: the AdCom rejection is expected to stand at the FDA decision. 'Probably' hedges; no PDUFA date given.

statements.quote: Thirteen million people in the US will have PTSD in any given year. 600/100,000 will have PTSD in their lifetime.
statements.context: Background on the PTSD burden in the brexpiprazole/sertraline AdCom post: 13 million Americans will have PTSD in any given year and 600 per 100,000 will have it in their lifetime, with a two times higher incidence in women, which the author attributes in part to child sexual abuse rates in girls.
statements.horizon_text: in any given year; in their lifetime
statements.note: Prevalence statistic phrased in future tense; not a forecast of change. Low forecast value.
